newsitem.title: UK: Chinese gold demand seen at 330 tonnes in '97 - UBS.
newsitem.headline: Chinese gold demand seen at 330 tonnes in '97 - UBS.

text.p: Chinese gold consumption could be about 330 tonnes in 1997 compared with a forecast 280 tonnes this year according to Andy Smith in Union Bank of Switzerland's latest Precious Metals Outlook.
Official estimates put Chinese gold demand at 400 tonnes a year from 1995 onwards, according to the publication.
Smith noted that new savings and investment opportunities for China's increasingly affluent population were distracting attention from gold's traditional store of value role.

The Chinese share market has grown rapidly and accounted for over $21 billion of "liquid savings" in about the first 11 months of 1996. Turnover on the market between January and August was more than double the whole of 1995.

Although the growth rate of private bank deposits in the third quarter, following an interest rate cut, halved compared with the rate in the first three months, it was still the equivalent of buying 520 tonnes of gold a month, Smith said.
The lower interest rate and subsequent drop in bank deposits could mean more people taking out life assurance rather than saving through gold.
Only nine percent of the inhabitants of the 50 major cities have life cover. A policy cost $36 a year, according to Smith.
The Chinese economy was developing resistance to the sort of financial shock which previously sent buyers looking for gold as a safe haven, he said.
Foreigh exchange reserves were almost $100 billion and 38 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) was in the service sector versus 15 percent in 1980.
Further, 20,000 financial institutions have sprung up to replace the state monopoly.
"It would be surprising if new gold offtake in 1996 escaped the hangover of inventory afflicting (a wide range of consumer goods)," Smith said.
Countering that to some extent, jeweller restocking, more visits to Hong Kong and share volatility may encourage some extra gold buying next year, he said.
Almost all China's gold will be imported -- officially or otherwise -- as China's gold production despite attempts to increase it, was only about 85 tonnes in 1996.
